articles.title: Nations expanding their research programmes impose sweeping penalties for malpractice
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02517-1India, Peru and Vietnam are rolling out policies that limit opportunities for scientists who fall foul of research-integrity guidelines.
articles.content:
In response to high retraction rates, India, Peru and Vietnam have introduced guidelines and disciplinary measures against research misconduct.Credit: designer491/iStock via Getty

In a bid to tighten research standards, governments and funders in countries with emerging research systems are increasingly rolling out disciplinary measures for researchers who do the wrong thing. The policies include docking bonuses, restricting access to grants and lowering the rankings of institutions linked to misconduct.

The reforms come as instances of research misconduct are on the rise worldwide. In May, for example, an audit1 of biomedical papers found that the rate of fabricated citations was 12 times greater in 2025 than in 2023. And later that month, an analysis2 of 33,000 cancer studies linked roughly 12% of them to suspected paper-mill activity.

The responsibility for cleaning up research malpractice has, for a long time, been a bottom-up affair: journal editors withdraw papers; universities investigate their staff members; and independent sleuths and organizations, such as Retraction Watch, expose what they can. Sometimes researchers will come forwards and correct the record themselves once they realize that they’ve made an error.

Retractions caused by honest mistakes are extremely stressful, say researchers

But there is a growing movement, particularly in countries with emerging research communities, to take a top-down approach. Funders and governments in some nations are increasingly restricting grants and opportunities for scientists who have been accused of research-integrity malpractice. These changes seek to cover a wide range of integrity issues, from plagiarism and falsified data to image manipulation and peer-review fraud.

Elisabeth Bik, an independent research-integrity consultant based in the the San Francisco Bay area, California, welcomes the roll-out of schemes that penalize malpractice in this way. “In order to tackle misconduct, there needs to be some type of sanction,” she says. “If there wasn’t the chance of getting a ticket, we’d all be speeding. There is fierce competition in science, and if people who cheat get better papers, then why not cheat yourself? We need to see that car being pulled over to warn other people.”

The top-down approach is needed, she says, because universities can be reluctant to sanction their own researchers, fearing that it will negatively affect their reputation. “Universities don’t do a great job in holding people accountable,” explains Bik. “It needs to be done by institutions with teeth.”

But how likely are these systems to deter dodgy science? And do they risk disincentivizing honest researchers from coming forwards and admitting to their mistakes?

Redesigning research rules

India — a nation that is rapidly rising through the ranks in the Nature Index — has initiated several measures to catch research malpractice.

The Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), one of India’s largest research funders, introduced rules in May that require applicants to disclose whether they have had a paper retracted in the past five years and explain why.

Applicants also need to testify that their grant proposals — or large parts of them — were not generated by artificial-intelligence tools. The ANRF has said that, in addition to these statements from researchers, it might use a combination of tools to screen for AI use in grant applications.

This follows an announcement last year that India’s National Institutional Ranking Framework, which publishes an official ranking of research organizations each year, will start to penalize institutions that have a large number of retracted papers, such as by giving them negative marks, affecting their total score.

The citation black market: schemes selling fake references alarm scientists

By making these changes, the Indian government is hoping to put pressure on universities to be proactive in preventing problematic research from being published in the first place, rather than responding once errors and wrongdoing are discovered, says Achal Agrawal, a data scientist based in Raipur, India. Agrawal founded India Research Watch, an online platform run by volunteers that tracks research-integrity issues.

“This feels significant because it’s the first step, and the first step is always the hardest,” says Agrawal, noting that more work is needed to ensure that there are long-term improvements in research conduct. The ANRF’s requirement that retractions be disclosed, for instance, is “just a voluntary disclosure, and it only lasts five years”, he says. Moreover, it’s not clear how the information provided by researchers will be verified. “But even just as a signal, even if they don’t implement it full-scale, I still think it’s quite significant,” he says.

Agrawal is optimistic that these measures are the beginning of a wider trend in India towards a top-down approach to research-integrity enforcement. “The ANRF is one of the biggest funding agencies in India, so this will probably have a ripple-on effect,” he says. “Institutes that want researchers to get grants will also probably be more careful when recruiting researchers.”

Ramping up

In Peru, another nation that has increased its efforts to combat research malpractice, researchers risk losing pay if they break the rules. The government announced in March that it will start docking the bonuses of researchers whose work is retracted in a bid to push back against those who engage in “acts that violate ethics and scientific integrity”.

Typically, Peruvian academics who participate in one or more research projects are eligible for monthly bonuses that range from 2,617 to 4,435 Peruvian soles (US$780 to $1,320), but those who have had one or more articles retracted in the past three years will no longer qualify.

The move follows a 2024 government investigation into alleged networks of paper mills in Peru. Percy Mayta-Tristán, vice-rector for research at the Scientific University of the South in Lima, says that the changes are needed. “We have good researchers, but we weren’t incentivizing research publication in a good way,” he says.

India to penalize universities with too many retractions

However, the system runs the risk of punishing researchers whose papers are retracted because of a genuine error or insufficient attention to methods transparency. For this reason, Bik says that she would like to see the reforms tweaked so that they differentiate between honest mistakes and wilful malpractice. “You want to encourage people who find a big error in their papers and retract it or republish it. That’s a good thing,” she says.

The Vietnamese government has also announced a framework on research integrity that will roll out a series of disciplinary actions for malpractice, including written warnings, mandatory public apologies and repayment of research funding. Violations will also be recorded on a national database.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on significant policy reforms by multiple nations to enforce research integrity through disciplinary measures, which promotes ethical scientific conduct and accountability. These top-down actions have broad societal impact by improving the reliability of scientific research globally, especially in emerging research systems. The story is focused and detailed, describing concrete steps taken by India, Peru, and Vietnam, and the expected positive effects on research standards.
articles.personality_title: India, Peru, and Vietnam introduce strict rules to stop scientific cheating
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Some countries are seeing more cases of scientists cheating by faking or copying research. This causes problems because science depends on honest work. Usually, journals and universities handle these issues, but now some governments want to take stronger actions.

**What happened** – India, Peru, and Vietnam have started new rules to punish researchers who break honesty rules. India requires scientists to report if their papers were withdrawn and checks if they use AI in grant proposals. Peru will reduce bonuses for scientists with retracted papers. Vietnam plans warnings, public apologies, and funding repayment for misconduct.

**Impact** – These rules are important because they encourage scientists and universities to be more careful and honest. India’s system also lowers the rankings of institutions with many retractions, which pushes universities to prevent cheating. Peru’s bonus cuts make researchers think twice before breaking rules. Vietnam’s national database will keep track of offenders. These efforts show a shift from relying on journals and universities alone to governments taking responsibility.

**What's next step** – Experts say these new policies need careful checking to avoid punishing honest mistakes. India’s rules may spread to more research groups and funding agencies. Peru and Vietnam will likely continue refining their systems to balance fairness with strong penalties. Over time, these changes could help build trust in science from countries that are growing their research programs.

**One-sentence takeaway** – India, Peru, and Vietnam are leading new efforts to stop scientific cheating by setting clear punishments that aim to improve honesty and trust in research.
articles.personality_title_fr: Inde, Pérou et Vietnam adoptent des règles strictes pour lutter contre la triche scientifique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Dans certains pays, on observe de plus en plus de cas de scientifiques trichant en falsifiant ou en copiant des recherches. Cela pose problème car la science repose sur l’honnêteté. Habituellement, les revues et universités traitent ces cas, mais désormais certains gouvernements veulent agir plus fermement.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – L’Inde, le Pérou et le Vietnam ont mis en place de nouvelles règles pour punir les chercheurs qui enfreignent les règles d’intégrité. L’Inde demande aux scientifiques de déclarer si leurs articles ont été retirés et contrôle l’usage de l’intelligence artificielle dans les demandes de subvention. Le Pérou réduit les primes des chercheurs avec des articles rétractés. Le Vietnam prévoit des avertissements, excuses publiques et remboursements des fonds en cas de faute.

**Impact** – Ces règles sont importantes car elles encouragent chercheurs et universités à être plus prudents et honnêtes. Le système indien baisse aussi le classement des institutions avec beaucoup de rétractations, ce qui pousse les universités à prévenir la triche. La réduction des primes au Pérou fait réfléchir avant d’enfreindre les règles. La base de données nationale du Vietnam suivra les contrevenants. Ces efforts montrent un passage de la gestion par revues et universités vers une responsabilité gouvernementale.

**Étape suivante** – Les experts disent que ces politiques doivent être surveillées pour éviter de punir les erreurs honnêtes. Les règles indiennes pourraient s’étendre à d’autres groupes de recherche et financeurs. Le Pérou et le Vietnam affineront leurs systèmes pour équilibrer justice et sanctions fortes. Avec le temps, ces changements pourraient renforcer la confiance dans la science dans ces pays en développement.

**Phrase-clé** – L’Inde, le Pérou et le Vietnam montrent la voie en luttant contre la triche scientifique grâce à des sanctions claires qui visent à améliorer l’honnêteté et la confiance dans la recherche.

articles.title: Gloria Steinem: A voice for women, to the very end
articles.summary: Gloria Steinem, the journalist and women's rights campaigner who became one of the most influential voices of the feminist movement, has died at the age of 92. In an announcement on Instagram, her family said she had passed away on Wednesday at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her.
articles.content:
Following news of her death, UN News revisits a powerful moment from Ms. Steinem's appearance at UN Headquarters in New York in 2016, when she took her message about violence against women to the global stage.

In her landmark speech ten years ago, the pioneering activist warned that violence against women is inseparable from questions of peace, security and democracy.

“The single most important element or determinant of whether a country is violent within itself or whether it will be willing to use military violence against another country is not poverty, not access to natural resources, not religion or even degree of democracy. It’s violence towards females.”

‘This is a world issue’

Ms. Steinem pointed to the many forms violence against women can take, from sexual violence in war – to trafficking, female genital mutilation (FGM) and violence in the home.

She also spoke about the consequences of cultures where sons are prioritised over daughters, and the resulting long-term impact on societies.

“This is not a women’s issue…Hello. This is not a children’s issue. This is a world’s issue.”

Violence against women remains a pervasive global public health and human rights concern.

According to the latest data from the gender equality agency UN Women, an estimated 840 million women – almost one in three – have been subjected to physical and/or sexual intimate partner violence, non-partner sexual violence, or both at least once in their life.

UN Photo/Teddy Chen

Legacy and inspiration

Ending violence against women and girls is central to the global effort to achieve gender equality and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

For Ms. Steinem, the treatment of women offered a revealing measure of the societies in which they lived.

“The easiest way to figure out how democratic and peaceful any group is, is to see: are there women there and how are they being treated?”

A lifetime of challenging inequality

Ms. Steinem became one of the most recognizable voices of the feminist movement in the United States during the 1960s and 1970s.

She helped highlight issues including reproductive rights, discrimination, political representation and violence against women – bringing them into the mainstream. She was also a co-founder of Ms. magazine and worked with generations of activists seeking greater equality.

Hope for humanity

Underlining that “each of us has some part of the knowledge, the solution, the insight, the understanding that will contribute to the whole”, she said that listening was key.

“You know, there’s nothing more important than listening to each other.”

In her later years, Ms. Steinem continued to write and to bring people together, including in her own New York home, creating regular “Talking Circles” – a tradition she wanted to continue beyond her lifetime, according to her family.

Stories from the UN Archive: Gloria Steinem takes to the world stage to call out violence against women
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.title: Cameroon’s indomitable Lionesses football team finally shatter WAFCON glass ceiling
articles.summary: After losing three finals, the Cameroonian women’s team finally lifted the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations. Their 3–0 victory over Malawi demonstrates this generation’s perseverance and progressive transformation in African women’s football.
articles.content:
After losing three finals, the Cameroonian women’s football team has finally lifted the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON). Their victory over Malawi in Rabat (the capital of Morocco) on August 16, 2026, stands as a testament to this generation’s perseverance and the progressive transformation of African women’s football.

For more than two decades, Cameroon has had a reputation for being a powerhouse in African women’s football, but they had never been able to go all the way and snag the coveted WAFCON trophy. However, Sunday, August 16, at the Moulay El Hassan Stadium, told an entirely different story. In the 2026 TotalEnergies Women’s Africa Cup of Nations final, the indomitable Lionesses beat Malawi 3–0, clinching their first-ever continental title.

Fourth final’s a charm

Before winning this championship title, Cameroon had already reached the WAFCON final in 2004, 2014, and 2016, losing each time to Nigeria without scoring a single goal. According to the official Confederation of African Football (CAF) statistics, the Lionesses hold the record for the most final appearances by a Central African nation.

Playing against Malawi in its first-ever WAFCON final, Cameroon left no room for doubt. In the 20th minute, Marie Ngah Manga scored the opening goal, before Naomi Najoah Eto doubled their lead nine minutes later with an acrobatic strike. Just before halftime, Ngah Manga scored a brace, with her second goal bringing the tally to 3–0. BeIN Sports provided detailed coverage of their victory, while sports website Yardbarker provided a tactical analysis.

At the final whistle, Cameroon was no longer a team that had never won the final, but the African champion. According to CAF, the country had now become the fourth African nation to lift this trophy, joining Nigeria (10 titles), Equatorial Guinea, and South Africa (2022).

Interestingly enough, Cameroon’s title journey has its own paradox. The country didn’t initially secure qualification on the pitch. As CameroonOnline reports, the team could only compete after the tournament expanded from 12 to 16 teams. Once in play, the Lionesses beat Ghana in the group stages, eliminated defending champion Nigeria 1-0 in the quarter-finals, and defeated host country Morocco on penalties in the semi-finals.

A generational handover

Cameroonian women’s football has long produced many players who ultimately become football legends, including Gabrielle Aboudi Onguéné. Today, a new generation has stepped up to take the mantle.

One of the team’s leading figures is Monique Ngock. This 21-year-old midfielder was named Woman of the Competition for her overall tournament performance. According to Yardbarker, she is best known for her tenacity, defensive anticipation, and composure on the ball.

Monique’s journey adds unique significance to this victory. At just 17, Monique had played in Cameroon’s 2022 quarter-final elimination match. Four years later, she is now one of the new African champions’ key players.

In an interview with CAF, quoted by Olympics.com, Ngock reflected on her initial lack of family support. She hopes this WAFCON title will show young girls watching African women’s football today that “girls can do anything.”

At this year’s WAFCON, Cameroonian players largely dominated the individual accolades. In addition to Ngock, goalkeeper Michaely Bihina, who played a decisive role in the semi-final penalty shootout against Morocco, earned the Best Goalkeeper Award. Also, according to The Ghana Report, Marie Ngah Manga was named Player of the Final. However, the Golden Boot, an award for the player who scores the most goals, went to Malawi’s Temwa Chawinga. Chawinga scored five goals and made two assists during her country’s tournament debut.

Cameroon’s triumph in Rabat comes at a time when African women’s football is still working to solidify its place, and the talent gap between nations continues to narrow. This final pitted two teams against each other that, ten years ago, wouldn’t have been among the favorites. Cameroon, which missed out on direct qualification, faced Malawi in its tournament debut. As the first final since 2022 to feature two teams that had never won the title, CAF hailed this final as historic event for both sides; one that crystalizes the emerging support for women’s football across the region.

How will Cameroon make the best of this landmark moment?

After the first few days of excitement that a continental trophy brings, the real challenge begins. This challenge means investing more in women’s leagues, improving preparation conditions, strengthening youth development, and ensuring visibility for female footballers without depending solely on major international tournaments.

In Rabat, the Lionesses overcame a 22-year-long struggle, transforming three lost finals, without scoring a single goal, into their first title win in no uncertain fashion.

Most importantly, they have given young girls watching from the country’s major cities, such as Yaoundé, Douala, Bafoussam, and elsewhere on the continent, a renewed vision of what African women’s football can be: A sport where champions and heroines are made.

Although this trophy has finally come to Cameroon, the next battle is ensuring this victory becomes a starting point, rather than a mere memory.

This milestone symbolizes progress in gender equality and empowerment in sports across Africa, with broad societal impact by inspiring young girls and promoting women's sports development.

articles.personality_title_fr: Les Lionnes du Cameroun remportent enfin leur premier titre de la Coupe d’Afrique des Nations féminine
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis plus de 20 ans, l’équipe féminine de football du Cameroun, surnommée les Lionnes, est l’une des plus fortes d’Afrique. Cependant, elles n’avaient jamais remporté la Coupe d’Afrique des Nations féminine (WAFCON), ayant perdu trois finales contre le Nigeria.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 16 août 2026, à Rabat au Maroc, le Cameroun a remporté pour la première fois la finale de la WAFCON en battant le Malawi 3-0. Marie Ngah Manga a marqué deux buts, et Naomi Najoah Eto un autre. Cette victoire est arrivée après que le Cameroun ait pu participer grâce à l’agrandissement du tournoi de 12 à 16 équipes. Elles ont battu des adversaires forts comme le Ghana, le Nigeria et le Maroc pour décrocher ce titre.

**Impact** – Cette victoire est historique car le Cameroun est devenu seulement le quatrième pays africain à remporter le trophée WAFCON. Cela montre la progression du football féminin africain et sa montée en compétitivité. Le succès de l’équipe met aussi en lumière une nouvelle génération de joueuses, comme Monique Ngock, élue meilleure joueuse du tournoi. Leur victoire inspire les jeunes filles au Cameroun et en Afrique en prouvant qu’avec du travail et du soutien, elles peuvent aussi réussir dans le sport.

**Prochaine étape** – Le Cameroun doit maintenant utiliser cette victoire pour améliorer le football féminin dans le pays. Cela signifie investir dans les championnats locaux, former les jeunes joueuses et assurer plus de visibilité et de soutien aux footballeuses, pas seulement pendant les grands tournois, mais toute l’année.

**Une phrase clé** – Après plusieurs finales perdues, les Lionnes du Cameroun ont remporté leur premier titre WAFCON, ouvrant un nouveau chapitre pour le football féminin en Afrique et inspirant les futures championnes.
articles.personality_title_es: Las Leonas de Camerún ganan su primer título de la Copa Africana Femenina
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante más de 20 años, el equipo femenino de fútbol de Camerún, conocido como las Leonas, ha sido uno de los más fuertes de África. Sin embargo, nunca habían ganado la Copa Africana de Naciones Femenina (WAFCON), perdiendo tres finales contra Nigeria.

**Qué pasó** – El 16 de agosto de 2026, en Rabat, Marruecos, Camerún ganó por primera vez la final de la WAFCON al vencer a Malawi 3-0. Marie Ngah Manga anotó dos goles y Naomi Najoah Eto uno. Esta victoria llegó después de que Camerún pudiera participar gracias a la ampliación del torneo de 12 a 16 equipos. Vencieron a rivales fuertes como Ghana, Nigeria y Marruecos para conseguir el título.

**Impacto** – Esta victoria es histórica porque Camerún se convirtió en solo el cuarto país africano en ganar el trofeo WAFCON. Muestra cómo el fútbol femenino africano está creciendo y volviéndose más competitivo. El éxito del equipo también destaca a una nueva generación de jugadoras, como Monique Ngock, nombrada Mejor Jugadora del torneo. Su triunfo inspira a las niñas jóvenes en Camerún y en toda África al demostrar que con esfuerzo y apoyo también pueden lograr grandes cosas en el deporte.

**Próximo paso** – Ahora Camerún enfrenta el reto de usar esta victoria para mejorar el fútbol femenino en el país. Esto significa invertir en ligas locales, formar a las jóvenes jugadoras y asegurar que las futbolistas reciban más atención y apoyo, no solo durante los grandes torneos, sino todo el año.

**Una frase clave** – Después de años de intentos fallidos, las Leonas de Camerún ganaron su primer título WAFCON, marcando un nuevo capítulo para el fútbol femenino en África e inspirando a futuras campeonas.
